analysis.one_liner: Directs EPA to set water pollution limits on PFAS chemicals discharged by major industries.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsor signed on before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the EPA to write, on a fixed schedule, federal limits on how much PFAS — long-lasting 'forever chemicals' linked to cancer and other health harms — can be discharged into rivers, lakes, and sewers by industries such as chemical and plastics plants, electroplating and metal finishing shops, textile mills, landfills, tanneries, paint makers, and plastics molders. It would also have required immediate monitoring of those discharges, locked in a standard EPA test method for detecting PFAS in water, and given $200 million a year to municipal wastewater plants to screen out industrial PFAS before it reaches waterways.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink from or live near waterways receiving industrial PFAS discharges. PFAS chemicals do not break down and accumulate in water supplies and the human body, so enforceable discharge limits and required monitoring would directly reduce one major route of contamination. Municipal wastewater utilities also benefit: they receive $200 million a year in grants to pretreat and trace industrial PFAS entering their systems, rather than bearing those cleanup costs alone.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to publish human health water quality criteria for every measurable PFAS substance or class within 3 years of enactment, giving states and regulators a federal health-based benchmark for these chemicals in water.

Requires the EPA to finalize effluent limitation guidelines — enforceable discharge limits — for eight polluting industry categories on a set schedule: organic chemicals, plastics and synthetic fibers, electroplating, and metal finishing by June 2025; textile mills and landfills by June 2026; and leather tanning, paint formulating, and plastics molding by June 2027.

Requires monitoring of PFAS discharges from those industries starting immediately upon enactment, and monitoring from pulp and paper mills, airports, and electrical component makers, with a decision due by the end of 2025 on whether to set limits for that second group.

Requires the EPA to formally promulgate its approved laboratory test method for PFAS in water, solids, and tissue by January 2025, making PFAS detection results legally reliable for permitting and enforcement.

Authorizes $200 million per year through fiscal 2028 in grants to publicly owned wastewater treatment works for pretreatment programs and local PFAS source tracking, shifting some of the cleanup burden off municipalities and water customers.

analysis.who_pays: Industries that discharge PFAS into water or sewers: chemical and plastics manufacturers, electroplating and metal finishing shops, textile mills, landfills, leather tanneries, paint formulators, and plastics molders would bear the cost of monitoring, treatment, and changing processes. The EPA would also need funding to write the rules. Some costs could ultimately reach consumers through product prices.

drawbacks.text: The new discharge limits would impose real compliance costs on the eight targeted industry categories, including treatment systems and process changes, and some of those costs could be passed to consumers in product prices.

The grant program for wastewater treatment plants is 'subject to the availability of appropriations,' so the $200 million annual authorization could exist on paper without Congress ever funding it, leaving utilities facing PFAS pretreatment duties without the promised money.

Only $12 million per year is authorized for the EPA's own work — writing water quality criteria and at least eight major rulemakings on fixed deadlines — a small amount for that regulatory workload, which could lead to rushed or legally vulnerable rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large and one-directional: PFAS are persistent, accumulate in bodies and water supplies, and industrial discharge is a controllable source. The costs fall on a small set of industries that profited from discharging these chemicals, though those costs are genuine and could reach consumers. The bill's main design weakness is underfunding — the EPA mandates and the municipal grant program depend on appropriations Congress would have had to pass separately.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2024 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which took no further action, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Clean Water Standards for PFAS Act of 2024 on April 18, 2024.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; that referral was the last recorded action.
The committee never held a hearing, reported the bill, or scheduled a vote, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that discharge PFAS into water — chemical and plastics makers, metal finishers, textile mills, landfills, tanneries, paint and plastics manufacturers — are better off, because they never faced the discharge limits, monitoring requirements, or compliance costs the bill would have imposed. Communities with PFAS-contaminated water gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee; found no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no senator besides the sponsor signed on, so the record shows only that the bill attracted no support from either party rather than an organized bloc of opposition.

industries.industry: Organic chemicals, plastics, and synthetic fiber manufacturers
industries.note: First in line for enforceable PFAS discharge limits by mid-2025 plus immediate monitoring. Their interest in avoiding treatment and redesign costs runs directly against the public's interest in cleaner water.
Facing PFAS discharge limits by June 2025 under the bill. Monitoring and treatment costs fall on these facilities; the benefit of reduced contamination flows to surrounding communities.
PFAS are widely used in fabric treatments, and the bill would have set discharge limits for mills by mid-2026. Compliance costs fall on the mills; cleaner water is a public benefit.
Landfill leachate is a major PFAS pathway to water, and the bill would have set discharge limits by mid-2026. Cost containment for landfill operators comes at the expense of water quality.

industries.industry: Leather tanneries, paint formulators, and plastics molders
industries.note: Three more categories that would have faced PFAS discharge limits by mid-2027 under the bill's schedule.

These public treatment plants currently absorb PFAS that industries send them and pass contaminated sludge and effluent downstream. The bill would have paid them $200 million a year to pretreat and trace PFAS instead of leaving that cost to water ratepayers.

industries.industry: Pulp, paper, airport, and electronics facilities
industries.note: They would have faced new monitoring requirements immediately and a decision by the end of 2025 on whether discharge limits would follow — an uncertain but potentially costly exposure.
